title: Guruship to the Granth
hookLine: the day in 1708 the Guru Granth Sahib became Guru is marked each autumn

cards: A community led by a living teacher meets a hard question sooner or later: what happens after? Who guides it when the teacher is gone?

For the Sikhs, that question came to a head in 1708, far from Punjab, at Nanded in the Deccan, by the Godavari river. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, had been gravely wounded. His four sons had all died before him.
The Sikhs around him asked who would guide them next. Today: Gurta Gaddi.

teach.h: GURTA GADDI: THE THRONE OF GURUSHIP.
teach.b: Gurta Gaddi means the throne of guruship: gaddi is the seat, the cushion of authority, and gurta is the office of the Guru. Sikh tradition remembers what happened at Nanded in 1708.

teach.h: NANDED: FIVE COINS AND A COCONUT.
teach.b: Guru Gobind Singh placed five coins and a coconut before the Granth, the same sign used when one Guru installed the next, and bowed to it. He declared that after him there would be no human Guru.
The Granth itself, now called the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the Guru: for Sikhs, not only a holy book, but the Guru, living in the Word.
Tradition says that not long before, at Damdama Sahib, the Granth had been completed with the hymns of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. So the Word was whole.
Sikhs also speak of the Guru Panth, the community of the Khalsa, as carrying the Guru's authority together, guided by the Granth.
After the Ardas, sangats often sing a couplet that says: by the command of the Timeless One the Panth was established; all Sikhs are commanded to accept the Granth as Guru.
That couplet comes from later Sikh writings rather than the Granth itself, but it puts the teaching in a line sangats sing together. What follows is simple and large.

teach.h: THE GURU IN EVERY SIKH'S REACH.
teach.b: In Sikh understanding, every Sikh, anywhere in the world, has direct access to the Guru.
No human successor stands between a Sikh and the Guru. Just the Word, opened each morning, read each night.
The Gurta Gaddi Divas is marked each autumn with kirtan, readings and processions, especially at Hazur Sahib in Nanded.

how: Sikhs mark Gurta Gaddi Divas each autumn with kirtan, readings and processions, especially at Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib in Nanded, where Guru Gobind Singh conferred guruship on the Granth in 1708.

games.q: it's 1708 at Nanded. the Tenth Guru is wounded, and his sons have all died. who does he name to guide the Sikhs?
games.why: he bowed to the Granth and named it Guru; Sikhs also speak of the Khalsa Panth carrying authority together, guided by it.

practice: If there's a Guru Granth Sahib or a gutka near you, bow to it, the way Sikhs do on entering the darbar; if not, picture the Granth on its raised seat, covered in cloth, a granthi waving the chaur above it, and bow your head toward that picture, slowly.
Let the bow mean: I'm ready to listen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you rise.

wordCard.voice: Gurta Gaddi. The throne of guruship, given by Guru Gobind Singh to the Granth at Nanded in 1708: from then on, Sikhs revere the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.

orig.note: Punjabi: the throne of guruship; gaddi is the seat of authority.

carryVoice: Your line: the eternal guru. The Word, whole, and in every Sikh's reach. See you tomorrow.
